analysis.one_liner: Bars FHA lenders from charging higher rates and fees on bigger mortgages and standardizes servicing fees.
analysis.headline: The bill never got past its first referral: it sat in the House Banking Committee and its housing subcommittee until the 101st Congress ended without any hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have changed the rules for lenders making government-insured mortgages. It would have banned lenders from charging higher interest rates, discount points, or fees simply because a borrower's loan amount was larger. It also would have required HUD to examine whether approved lenders were actually meeting the mortgage needs of their communities, including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods, and to publish corrective plans from lenders that fell short, with public comment. Finally, it would have set a standardized, capped fee for servicing government-guaranteed mortgages.
analysis.who_benefits: FHA-insured homebuyers, especially in low- and moderate-income neighborhoods, would pay lower fees and face lenders held accountable for serving their community. Residents of under-served neighborhoods would gain a way to trigger an official examination of a lender's record.

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits lenders from varying the interest rate, discount points, loan origination fee, or other charges based on the size of the insured loan, ending a practice that raised costs for borrowers taking larger FHA mortgages.

It requires HUD, during examinations of approved mortgagees, to assess whether each lender is meeting the residential lending needs of its community, including neighborhoods of predominantly low- and moderate-income families, and to weigh that record in deciding whether the lender stays approved for FHA insurance programs.

Lenders found deficient would have to file a remediation plan, published in the Federal Register and local newspapers, with a 60-day public comment period; continued failure could cost a lender its FHA approval or limit its participation, and any person could request an examination of a lender's community lending record.
It standardizes servicing fees on government-guaranteed mortgage securities at 44 hundredths of one percent of outstanding principal, limiting what servicers can charge and retain.

analysis.who_pays: FHA-approved mortgage lenders would face new cost restrictions and performance reviews, and could lose their FHA approval if they under-serve their communities. Mortgage servicers would have their compensation standardized and capped, remitting any excess collections to the Government National Mortgage Association.

drawbacks.text: Setting a uniform servicing fee, calculated by the Secretary and reconciled annually with federal appropriations to top up shortfalls, would replace market-based pricing with a fixed government rate, and the bill authorizes appropriations for a revolving fund to pay servicers when collections fall short, creating a taxpayer backstop.

Lenders argue that pricing loans partly by size reflects the cost of making bigger loans, and that banning size-based variation could shift costs onto other borrowers or make some FHA lending less attractive; the performance-review system also adds regulatory burden that could discourage lenders from participating in FHA programs at all, narrowing credit options.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For borrowers, the fee and pricing protections are straightforward and the public-review mechanism gives communities real leverage over under-serving lenders. The standardization section is the weakest part: it hard-wires a fixed servicing fee with a federal appropriations safety net, trading predictability for rigidity. On balance the bill's consumer protections outweigh the design flaws, but it was never debated, so no committee ever weighed these trade-offs on the record.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Banking Committee, then to its housing subcommittee two weeks later, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Tom Ridge and Representative Mary Rose Oakar introduced the bill on October 31, 1989, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Banking, Finance and Urban Affairs.
On November 15, 1989, it was referred to the committee's Subcommittee on Housing and Community Development, and no further action was recorded for the rest of the 101st Congress.
The bill attracted only one cosponsor, a single House Democrat, and never advanced to a committee markup or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: FHA-approved mortgage lenders and mortgage servicers are better off, since the fee restrictions, community lending reviews, and servicing fee caps never took effect. FHA borrowers in under-served neighborhoods gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Tom Ridge
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Neighborhood Mortgage Lenders Accountability Act and steered it to the Banking Committee.

for.name: Rep. Mary Rose Oakar
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction as its only Democratic cosponsor alongside one additional Democratic cosponsor.

against.name: House Committee on Banking, Finance and Urban Affairs
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on introduction and never took it up for a markup or reported it to the floor before the Congress ended.

against.name: Subcommittee on Housing and Community Development
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on November 15, 1989 and held no recorded action on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a Republican sponsor and only two Democratic cosponsors and died in committee, so no vote ever showed where the parties stood.

industries.note: The bill would bar lenders from scaling rates, points, and fees to loan size and would expose them to community-lending reviews that could cost them FHA approval. Their interest in defeating it ran against borrowers in low- and moderate-income neighborhoods, who pay the size-based fees the bill targeted.

industries.industry: Mortgage servicers and GNMA securities issuers
industries.note: The bill would set a fixed 44-basis-point servicing fee, capping what servicers keep on government-guaranteed mortgage pools while guaranteeing them a defined compensation stream, with any shortfall made up from a federally funded revolving account. Servicing revenue would be locked in by statute but no longer expandable beyond the set rate.
